questions.stem: The irrational fear of heights is called:

options.option_text: Claustrophobia
Acrophobia
Xenophobia
Hydrophobia

questions.explanation: Acro- (Greek: 'height, summit') + phobia. Claustrophobia — enclosed spaces. Xenophobia — foreigners / strangers. Hydrophobia — water (also a classic symptom of rabies, which is why the disease itself is sometimes called hydrophobia). Agoraphobia — open / public spaces.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Snakes
Spiders
Germs
Crowds

questions.explanation: Arachne (Greek: spider) + phobia. Spielberg's 1990 film 'Arachnophobia' used the word as its title. Fear of snakes = ophidiophobia. Fear of germs = mysophobia (germophobia). Fear of crowds = enochlophobia / demophobia. Fear of public speaking (very high-hit) = glossophobia.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Closed spaces
Open or public spaces
Heights
Darkness

questions.explanation: Agora (Greek: open marketplace, public gathering place) + phobia. Sufferers feel panic in crowded public places and often in places from which escape may be difficult. Claustrophobia is the opposite — fear of closed / small spaces (elevators, MRIs). Fear of darkness = nyctophobia.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: An obsession or craze for books — especially for collecting them — is called:

options.option_text: Kleptomania
Bibliomania
Pyromania
Egomania

questions.explanation: 'Biblio' — book; 'mania' — obsessive desire or madness. Kleptomania — compulsion to steal (even trivial things). Pyromania — compulsion to start fires. Egomania — obsessive self-centredness. Megalomania — grandiose delusions. The '-phile' form gives 'bibliophile' (book-lover, without the pathology).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: The fear of being in enclosed or confined spaces is called:

options.option_text: Agoraphobia
Claustrophobia
Acrophobia
Xenophobia

questions.explanation: Latin 'claustrum' (enclosed space) + Greek 'phobia'. Common triggers — elevators, MRI machines, small rooms, aircraft cabins. Different from agoraphobia (opposite: fear of open / public places). Acrophobia — heights. Xenophobia — strangers / foreigners.
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: Match the phobia with its trigger. A. Hydrophobia. B. Ophidiophobia. C. Triskaidekaphobia. D. Glossophobia. List-II: 1. Water, 2. Snakes, 3. Number 13, 4. Public speaking.
questions.explanation: Hydro- = water; ophid- = snake (Greek 'ophis'); triskaideka- = 13 (Greek); glosso- = tongue (hence public speaking). Other niche ones to know — technophobia (technology), xenophobia (strangers/foreigners), photophobia (light — a symptom as well), thanatophobia (death), astraphobia (lightning / thunder).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

options.option_text: Suffers from split personality
Has delusions of grandeur or power
Compulsively steals small items
Has an irrational fear of big objects

questions.explanation: Megalo- (Greek 'megas': great) + mania (madness, obsession). A megalomaniac has an exaggerated belief in their own importance, power or grandeur. Split personality / dissociative identity disorder is a different condition. Compulsive stealing = kleptomania. Fear of big objects = megalophobia (technically).
questions.subject: Vocabulary

questions.stem: A person with an intense, irrational dread of darkness or the night is said to suffer from which condition?

options.option_text: Heliophobia — abnormal dread of sunlight or solar exposure
Nyctophobia — abnormal dread of darkness and the night
Thalassophobia — abnormal dread of deep sea or ocean depths
Dendrophobia — abnormal dread of trees and forested areas

questions.explanation: Nyctophobia (Greek 'nyx' = night) is the irrational fear of darkness or the night. Heliophobia is a frequent distractor here as it sounds vaguely night-related, but it actually means the fear of sunlight — the exact opposite trigger.

questions.stem: Which term describes a compulsive, irresistible impulse to steal items — regardless of their monetary value or personal need?

options.option_text: Dipsomania — uncontrollable compulsive craving for alcoholic drinks
Erotomania — delusional conviction of being romantically pursued
Kleptomania — irresistible impulse to steal without financial motive
Pyromania — obsessive compulsion to deliberately set fires ablaze

questions.explanation: Kleptomania (Greek 'kleptein' = to steal) is the compulsive urge to steal for the act itself, not for monetary gain. Pyromania is a common wrong answer because both are classified as impulse-control disorders, but pyromania specifically concerns fire-setting.

questions.stem: A person suffering from 'dipsomania' is best characterised by which of the following conditions?

options.option_text: An obsessive desire to roam and travel from place to place
An uncontrollable, episodic craving for alcoholic beverages
An irrational and persistent fear of open bodies of water
A compulsive tendency to hoard and accumulate miscellaneous objects

questions.explanation: Dipsomania (Greek 'dipsa' = thirst) refers to periodic, uncontrollable bouts of craving for alcohol — distinct from general alcoholism in its episodic nature. Option A describes dromomania; Option C describes thalassophobia — both planted as plausible traps.

questions.stem: Which psychiatric term describes a pathological, compulsive urge to wander or travel — typically with no fixed destination or rational purpose?

options.option_text: Ergomania — an obsessive and all-consuming devotion to one's work
Dromomania — a compulsive and uncontrollable urge to wander far
Oniomania — a compulsive and addictive urge to shop or purchase
Plutomania — an obsessive mania for accumulating personal wealth

questions.explanation: Dromomania (Greek 'dromos' = running/racecourse) is the compulsion to wander. Ergomania and oniomania are real terms (work and shopping respectively) inserted as distractors since candidates who know one mania may confuse the 'drom-' prefix with motion-related ergo or onion.

questions.stem: In clinical psychology, 'erotomania' is a delusional disorder in which the patient falsely and fixedly believes that:

options.option_text: romantic love is a psychologically devastating and perilous pursuit
a person of higher social status is secretly in love with the patient
every person they encounter is romantically attracted to them
their own romantic feelings are symptoms of an underlying mental illness

questions.explanation: Erotomania (de Clérambault's syndrome) is the specific delusion that one particular person — typically of higher status — is secretly in love with the patient. Option C is the most tempting wrong answer: candidates assume it means 'everyone loves me', but the clinical definition centres on one idealised, specific individual.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly pairs both the phobia and the mania derived from the same Greek root 'ergon' (meaning work)?

options.option_text: Ergophobia: fear of work; Ergomania: an obsession with cleanliness
Ergophobia: fear of work; Ergomania: an obsessive devotion to work
Ergophobia: fear of strangers; Ergomania: obsession with earnings
Ergophobia: fear of physical pain; Ergomania: obsession with effort

questions.explanation: Both terms share the root 'ergon' (work): ergophobia is the irrational fear of work or activity, while ergomania is the obsessive, pathological devotion to work — the polar opposite on the same axis. Option A is the key trap: it maps ergomania to cleanliness, which is actually ablutomania — a plausible slip for candidates who know ablutomania but misremember the root.

questions.stem: The clinical term 'mythomania' — also known as pseudologia fantastica — correctly refers to which psychological condition?

options.option_text: An extreme irrational fear of myths, folklore, and supernatural tales
An obsessive preoccupation with studying ancient myths and legends
A compulsive, pathological tendency to lie, exaggerate, or fabricate
A delusional belief that one is a character from ancient mythology

questions.explanation: Mythomania (from 'mythos' = fabricated story/lie) is the compulsive habit of telling elaborate falsehoods, also clinically termed pseudologia fantastica. Options A and B are the primary traps: 'mytho-' naturally evokes mythology, but in psychiatric vocabulary it denotes invented narrative, not the study of myths. Candidates who have not seen the synonym 'pseudologia fantastica' will be misled.
